newsitem.title: THAILAND: Creditwatch on Thai ratings not surprising.
newsitem.headline: Creditwatch on Thai ratings not surprising.

text.p: Standard and Poor's decision to put a negative creditwatch on the Thai foreign currency rating is not surprising, but will add pressure on the government to implement adequate measures to help the economy, analysts said on Friday.

Standard & Poor's Corp said on Friday it placed Thailand's "A" long-term foreign currency rating on creditwatch with negative implications. It said about $3 billion of foreign currency debt was affected.
It also placed Thailand's "AA" long-term local currency credit rating on creditwatch with negative implications.
"The S&P decision is actually appropriate," said an analyst at Seamico Securities Plc. "With all its current problems, Thailand does not deserve an 'A'."

Many other analysts agreed, noting that Thailand's decision last week to seek advice and possible financial assistance from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was a sign of the extent of the country's financial difficulties.
"Thailand's decision to go to the IMF amounts to an admission that its policies do not work," the Seamico analyst said.
"It's hardly surprising," said one foreign analyst. "Obviously, people are going to be looking at things very closely and all eyes will be on the government next week."

The government is due to announce on Tuesday a series of measures aimed at boosting the economy, which is growing at its slowest pace in a decade amid slowing exports and a liquidity crunch in the financial sector, which is already over-exposed to the cash-strapped ailing property market.
Thailand is also saddled with about $90 billion in foreign debt, about $40 billion of which is short-term and comes due by the end of the year.
The package to be announced by Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya is expected to be in line with IMF recommendations on tough measures Thailand needs to take to boost the economy.
It is not yet clear if it will include the announcement of any IMF loans or standby credit lines.

S&P said in a statement that the creditwatch reflected greater-than-expected loan losses in the financial sector that were expected to put a sizeable fiscal burden on the government and lead to weakened economic growth for several years.
S&P also placed the ratings of eight financial institutions, including the country's largest bank, Bangkok Bank Plc, on negative creditwatch.
"The rating actions reflect Standard & Poor's concerns that non-performing loans and loan losses will rise to levels not consistent with current ratings," S&P said.

The rating agency said the creditwatch on the currency reflected the coalition government's slow response to the economic problems and its failure to effectively manage problems in the financial sector.

In the past week alone, there has been a major upheaval among top financial authorities as the central bank governor and the permanent secretary of the finance ministry were replaced. In June, the finance minister resigned over policy conflicts.
"What can surprise one anymore? Is there anything potentially in this market at all that in any way could really shock you?" said Russel Kopp, head of research at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
